Lay
lā
v. (to put or place down; to set in position; rendering Hebrew yacad, suwm, Greek tithemi)
From Saxon lecgan, to place. Scripture's two great uses are architectural and sacrificial: God lays a foundation stone in Zion, and the Good Shepherd lays down His life.

Biblical Definition

To lay is to set a thing deliberately in its place, and Scripture's first great use is architectural. The LORD announces what He Himself will put down: “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation: he that believeth shall not make haste” (Isaiah 28:16). Each word is load-bearing — tried, because the stone has been proved; precious, because of its worth; sure, because what rests on it will stand — and the response required is belief rather than haste. The Apostle identifies the stone and forbids competitors: “other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:11). Men may build well or badly on it, but no man may lay another. The second great use is sacrificial, and our Lord makes it the mark of the true shepherd against the hireling: “Therefore doth my Father love me, because I lay down my life, that I might take it again” (John 10:17). The laying down is voluntary, and it is paired with a taking again, so that the cross is never separated from the resurrection. The same verb measures His poverty in the days of His flesh: “the Son of man hath not where to lay his head” (Matthew 8:20).

Webster 1828 Definition

To place in a lying position; to set or put down; to deposit; to impose or charge. Scripture's weightiest uses are the foundation stone God lays in Zion and the life the Good Shepherd lays down of Himself.

expand to see more

LAY, v.t. [Sax. lecgan, to place.] To place in a lying position; to set or place in a horizontal direction; as, to lay a book on the table.

2. To put or place in general; to deposit; as, to lay a foundation.

3. To impose, as a burden, tax, duty or command; as, to lay a tax on land.

4. To spread on a surface; as, to lay colors on canvas.

5. To bring forth and deposit, as eggs.

6. To wager; to stake; as, to lay a sum of money on the event.

LAY, v.i. To bring forth eggs. To wager or bet. [Note: to lay is transitive; to lie is intransitive.]

Key Scripture

Isaiah 28:16 — "Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD, Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation: he that believeth shall not make haste."

1 Corinthians 3:11 — "For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ."

John 10:17 — "Therefore doth my Father love me, because I lay down my life, that I might take it again."

Matthew 8:20 — "And Jesus saith unto him, The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head."

Modern Corruption

Foundations are treated as interchangeable — a church may be built on vision, personality, or cause — where Scripture says the only foundation is already laid and no man may lay another.

expand to see more

The practical error of the age is not usually a denial that Christ is the foundation but a quiet addition of others beside Him. A congregation is founded on a man's gifts, a movement on a grievance, a ministry on a method, and Christ is confessed at the level of doctrine while something else bears the actual weight. 1 Corinthians 3:11 addresses exactly that situation: Paul is writing to a church dividing over teachers, and he does not say that Christ is the best foundation among several but that no other can be laid. The test is simple — remove the man, the cause, or the method, and see whether the building stands.

A second corruption touches John 10:17. The laying down of Christ's life is often described as a tragedy He suffered rather than an act He performed, and the words that follow in the passage are dropped: no man taketh it from Him; He lays it down of Himself, and He has power to take it again. That voluntary character is what makes the cross an offering rather than a martyrdom, and it is the ground of the Father's stated love. Recover it, and the shepherd's laying down of His life stands over against every hireling who flees.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yacad (to found, lay a foundation) governs Isaiah 28:16; suwm (to put, place, set) is the common verb of placing; Greek tithemi (to put, place, lay down) covers both foundation-laying and the laying down of life.

expand to see more

Hebrew yacad (H3245) — to found, to lay a foundation; the verb of the tried stone laid in Zion.

Hebrew suwm (H7760) — to put, place, set, appoint; the ordinary verb of laying a thing in its place.

Hebrew pinnah (H6438) — corner; the source of the corner stone figure that Isaiah and the Apostles apply to Christ.

Greek tithemi (G5087) — to place, to lay down; used of laying a foundation and of Christ laying down His life.

Greek themelios (G2310) — a foundation; the noun of 1 Corinthians 3:11, which no man may re-lay.

Usage

"“Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone” — the foundation is God's own placing, not the builders'."

"“Other foundation can no man lay” — the exclusion is of possibility, not merely of preference."

"“I lay down my life, that I might take it again” — the offering is voluntary and paired with the resurrection."
